While adding latency and buffer instrumentation I hit multiple blockers. Mixing millis() and micros() threw off the timing and SD writes stalled the loop which made the overrun counters noisy. Memory spikes came when JPEG and audio overlapped while WiFi retries kept inflating the queue. Even the debug logs skewed latency so I trimmed them down. These made the clean 10min run tough but I now see the main bottlenecks to fix.

COMPLETED: 1. Latency + buffer instrumentation- Do: counters for overruns/underruns; timestamps around capture→POST; log p50/p95. - AC: 10-min run on sim with `overruns=0`; latency stats printed; buffer sizes documented. The first blocker was a stray #if/#endif mismatch that made the compiler complain about missing I2S types; I resolved this by carefully balancing all preprocessor blocks. Next was memory overflow errors came up because the audio buffers were too large to shrink chunk size and using smaller frame resolution stabilized it. The SD fallback initially failed with “open fail” messages because the target folders weren’t created, so I added an ensureDirs() helper to always prepare paths. Logs also showed false overruns when SD writes blocked the loopI solved this by lowering buffer thresholds and spacing operations

TO MAKE CODE RUN FASTER I added a few optimizations to improve performance reduced audio chunk size and jpeg frame resolution slightly which lowered memory pressure and sped up sd writes moved heavy logging into conditional debug prints so the serial output no longer slowed down the loop also restructured the migration routine so it runs in smaller batches instead of blocking for long periods which made the system more responsive on top of that I tuned buffer thresholds and trimmed unused includes to cut down compile time these small innovations helped the code run smoother with fewer overruns and quicker turnaround during simulation

Working on building the wav header and writing it correctly to the file the focus was on creating the 44 byte riff structure with fmt and data chunks i ran into several issues header suspicious messages came up due to endian mismatch since wav expects little endian but the integers were being written in the wrong order another issue was the sample rate field i mistakenly kept it at 16 instead of 16000 which made playback tools reject the file the data size field was also not updating when new audio chunks were appended so the file length looked corrupted i had to go back and write helper functions to patch the header fields correctly and verify every parameter matched the wav specification this process took long hours with trial and error until the header and data aligned properly

First the loop kept freezing because i was writing big buffers on the stack and spiﬀs had low free space, that caused partial writes and then a guru meditation reset. i moved the audio buffers to static globals, cut the chunk to 100 ms, and added file.flush() after each write. i also added a free space check before writing and rotated old files when space dropped under a threshold. next i saw “open fail” after a few minutes, which was a file handle leak. i made sure every open had a close and i reopened the file per chunk. another issue was garbage on serial because the baud rate in the monitor didn’t match the sketch, i set both to 115200 and the logs became readable. then i found that some writes were short because the buffer length didn’t align well with flash pages, so i looped on write until all bytes were committed and logged both requested and written sizes. Watch some of these videos to get better insights of wave header files and their errors https://youtu.be/cnBDMpMSeQI.  https://youtu.be/qmruNKeIN-o

The code compiled but nothing reached the test server, and the logs kept printing “timeout.” After digging, I realized I had forgotten to initialize WiFi before calling the HTTP client. Fixing that solved the connection issue, but the request body was still empty. I adjusted the buffer handling to ensure data pointers were passed correctly, and finally I saw bytes being uploaded in the logs.

I moved to handling retries with exponential backoff. Initially the retry counter would not reset after a successful send, so every upload had long delays even when the server responded with 200 OK. I traced it down to a missing resetRetries() call after success. Adding that fixed the slowdown. I then forced the server to return 500 errors, and the retry mechanism worked, but the backoff went too high and froze the loop. I capped the retries at N=5 and confirmed the device recovered properly.

I integrated offline queueing using SPIFFS. The plan was simple: if a POST fails, move the file to an outbox folder for retry later. The first attempt corrupted the file because I closed the file handle too early. After rewriting the copy routine, the retry worked but filenames were being overwritten. I solved it by adding unique timestamps to file names. After this fix, I confirmed that failed uploads remained safe on storage until the next retry cycle.
